facts.title: Named After A Swedish Village
facts.text: Terbium owes its name to Ytterby, a tiny quarry village near Stockholm, Sweden. That single mine is the source of four element names — terbium, yttrium, erbium, and ytterbium — more than any other place on Earth. Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander first separated terbium from yttria there in 1843.

facts.title: A Confusing Identity Swap
facts.text: For decades after its discovery, chemists mixed up the names of terbium and erbium because both were faint impurities hidden in the same ore. The labels were actually swapped around 1860, so the substance we now call terbium briefly carried the name erbium and vice versa. It took the new tool of spectroscopy in the 1860s and 1870s to finally sort the rare-earth siblings apart.

facts.title: The Glow Behind Your Screen
facts.text: Terbium is one of the most important phosphor activators ever found, producing an intense, pure green light when struck by electrons or ultraviolet rays. For years it created the green pixels in cathode-ray-tube televisions and the green band in fluorescent lamps and trichromatic white LEDs. A common green phosphor is terbium-doped, often written as Tb:Y2O3 or in compounds like LaPO4:Ce,Tb.

facts.title: A Metal That Stretches In A Magnet
facts.text: Terbium is a star ingredient in Terfenol-D, an alloy of terbium, dysprosium and iron that shows giant magnetostriction — it physically changes shape in a magnetic field far more than ordinary materials. This lets it convert electricity into precise mechanical motion, powering sonar transducers, ultra-precise actuators and even speakers that turn a flat surface into a loudspeaker. The effect is large enough to be useful in real machinery, not just laboratory curiosities.

facts.title: Soft Enough To Cut
facts.text: Despite being a metal, pure terbium is silvery-gray and soft enough to be cut with a knife. It is malleable and ductile, and freshly exposed surfaces slowly tarnish in air as they react with oxygen. Like its rare-earth cousins, it is reactive enough that it must be handled and stored carefully to keep it from oxidizing.

facts.title: Magnetism That Switches With Temperature
facts.text: Terbium has remarkable magnetic behavior that depends sharply on temperature. Below about 219 kelvin (roughly minus 54 degrees Celsius) it becomes ferromagnetic, and between there and around 230 kelvin it passes through a more exotic antiferromagnetic, helical magnetic state. This temperature-tuned magnetism makes it a valuable subject for studying how magnetic order arises in matter.

facts.title: Forged In Dying Stars
facts.text: Terbium is not made on Earth — its atoms were created in violent cosmic events, chiefly the rapid neutron capture process during supernova explosions and merging neutron stars. As a result it is genuinely rare in the universe and even rarer than many lighter elements. Every gram on our planet is stardust that was incorporated into the rock when the solar system formed.

facts.title: Rarer Than You'd Guess, Yet Everywhere
facts.text: Terbium makes up only about 1.2 parts per million of Earth's crust, making it one of the scarcer rare-earth elements. It is never found as a free metal in nature, instead hiding in minerals such as monazite, bastnasite, xenotime and cerite. Most commercial terbium today is extracted as a small fraction of the rare earths mined from deposits like Bayan Obo in Inner Mongolia, China.

facts.title: A Beacon For Doctors
facts.text: Terbium has become a rising star in nuclear medicine because it offers a rare quartet of useful radioactive isotopes. Terbium-149, terbium-152, terbium-155 and terbium-161 can be used for PET and SPECT imaging as well as for alpha and beta cancer therapy, letting doctors potentially image and treat tumors with chemically identical tracers. Researchers call this matched set a true theranostic toolkit, all built from one element.

facts.title: Glowing Tags In The Lab
facts.text: Terbium ions emit sharp, long-lived green fluorescence, which scientists exploit as molecular flashlights in biology and chemistry. Because the glow persists for milliseconds — far longer than ordinary background fluorescence — researchers can time their measurements to filter out noise in highly sensitive assays. Terbium-based labels are used to detect proteins, DNA and trace metals with great precision.
